chunks: "The idea is that a MOSFET that's fully on is basically a small resistor, R DS(on) . So if I measure the drain-source voltage while it's conducting, I equals V DS over R DS(on) .
There's nothing to add to the circuit and no extra loss, because the FET is already in the current path.
In practice I run V DS into a comparator or amplifier with a threshold and use it for overcurrent protection, which is how many motor driver and hot-swap ICs do desaturation or V DS monitoring.
The pros are zero extra loss, no extra component or board space, very fast response, and it can scale automatically with the FET. The cons are accuracy and conditions.
R DS(on) rises a lot with temperature, perhaps 50 percent or more at 125 degrees, and varies part to part, so my threshold might correspond to 20 amps cold and 14 amps hot.
It only works when the FET is fully on, so I have to blank the switching edges, and during the off-time or when the body diode conducts the reading is meaningless.
And with very low R DS(on) the signal is only tens of millivolts, so comparator offset matters.
So it's great for protection, where plus or minus 30 percent is acceptable, and not for precise measurement unless I calibrate and compensate for temperature."
